Consumer complaint narrative: Complaint Against Bank of America - Adverse Credit Reporting Following Autopay Cancellation Without Notice Summary I have been a Bank of America customer since XXXX, with two credit cards and an unblemished payment history that helped me build and maintain a XXXX score in the XXXX for many years. In XX/XX/XXXX, Bank of America reported a 30-day late payment to all three credit bureaus on a {$10.00} balance - the first late payment of my life- after their own system cancelled my long-standing autopay arrangement without notifying me. I learned of the delinquency not from Bank of America, but from a competitor 's credit monitoring service, the day after the damage had already been reported. Bank of America has since refused, in writing, to correct it. Background I have lived overseas for the past five years and relied on autopay precisely so that routine payments would never be missed. Bank of America 's own email records confirm that my autopay operated every month without interruption from XX/XX/XXXX through XX/XX/XXXX - more than six and a half years- funded from my external XXXX account. In XX/XX/XXXX, it stopped. I received no email, no letter, and no notification of any kind that the arrangement had been cancelled. The first indication I had that anything was wrong came on XX/XX/XXXX at XXXX XXXX, in an alert from XXXX XXXX XXXX- a credit monitoring service operated by a competitor - informing me that one of my accounts was more than 30 days past due. By then, Bank of America had already reported a 30-day late payment to all three bureaus- on a {$10.00} balance, after thirteen years of on-time payments. My XXXX score fell from approximately XXXX to XXXX. I would have prevented this, and I can prove it Bank of America had every means to reach me and used them constantly- for everything except the one notification that mattered. They had my correct email address, which they used throughout this period for statements, XXXX score reminders, fraud alerts, and marketing. They had my correct US mailing address, a service I pay for, and which I confirmed with the provider was working and received nothing from Bank of America about this matter. The channels functioned. Bank of America simply did not use them to tell me my autopay had been cancelled, that a balance was overdue, or that my credit was about to be affected. I can demonstrate that timely notice would have prevented the harm entirely, because my two cards became an unintended controlled experiment. Both lost autopay at the same time, from the same funding source. The only difference between them was their statement closing dates : Card XXXX closes on the XXXX of the month ; Card XXXX closes on the XXXX. Card XXXX closed delinquent on XX/XX/XXXX and was reported on XX/XX/XXXX- before I knew anything was wrong. By the time XXXX alerted me on XX/XX/XXXX, it was too late to prevent it. But I acted immediately : I manually posted a payment to Card XXXX on XX/XX/XXXX, XXXX days before its XX/XX/XXXX closing date, and that card was never reported late. The difference was not my conduct. It was six days on a calendar, and the fact that I happened to discover the problem in time to save one card but not the other. The moment I learned of the issue, I resolved it. I would have done the same for Card XXXX had Bank of America given me any notice before XX/XX/XXXX. Card XXXX is direct proof that a single timely notification would have prevented all of this. What Bank of America 's representatives confirmed I called on XX/XX/XXXX and spoke first with a representative named XXXX, then a supervisor named XXXX, who was dismissive, declined to investigate the cause, told me the matter was my responsibility, and offered only to help me pay the balance and re-enable autopay. That call was not recorded. I called again on XX/XX/XXXX and recorded the calls with notice to each representative. After XXXX in North Carolina helped me close my savings account, I was connected to XXXX in the XXXX, New York office, who reviewed my account and stated : " We have been migrating all of our clients over to the new payment system online ... that does look like that happened in XXXX for you so that's when that was cancelled... It was a system event because we moved everybody over from one our payment platform to our new payment platform ... All of our clients that have cards are going to be affected by this. '' XXXX transferred me to XXXX, who consulted her online banking team and said I " should have received '' a website pop-up, a formal letter, and a phone alert - but could not confirm that any had actually been sent or delivered to me. I told her, on the recording, that I had checked my email including spam and junk folders and found nothing, and she did not dispute it. The " phone alert '' presumes an app I do not have installed and never agreed to receive notices through. The " formal letter, '' per my mail provider, never arrived. XXXX also stated that one of my cards " had never been set up on autopay '' - which Bank of America 's own back office contradicted. XXXX in Alabama investigated and confirmed : " They were able to see that it was set up before from your XXXX ending in XXXXXXXX Yes, they were able to confirm that it was for both [ accounts ]. '' XXXX began filing credit correction requests for both cards, but the call disconnected at the 30-minute mark, before she could finish. When I called back on XX/XX/XXXX, XXXX initially offered to continue XXXX 's work, then returned to the same position as the dismissive supervisor : that the matter was my responsibility, that nothing had been filed, and that all required notifications had been sent. I informed him I would be filing a formal complaint. Bank of America 's own records contradict their notification claims Bank of America maintains that notifications were sent. Their own email history shows otherwise : XX/XX/XXXX : the final " automatic payment scheduled '' email - the last in a monthly sequence spanning six and a half years. XX/XX/XXXX to XX/XX/XXXX : a continuous stream of routine emails - statements, XXXX reminders, fraud alerts, marketing- with no message referencing autopay cancellation, a past-due balance, or impending credit reporting. XX/XX/XXXX : Card XXXX reaches 30 days past due. XX/XX/XXXX : Bank of America reports it to all three bureaus. XX/XX/XXXX : a competitor 's monitoring service notifies me. XX/XX/XXXX : Bank of America sends a " Bill Pay service deactivated '' email - five days after reporting me. XX/XX/XXXX : Bank of America sends an " ACTION NEEDED- Before XX/XX/XXXX '' migration email - nine days after the damage was done. Bank of America clearly has the capability to warn customers about exactly this kind of change. In XX/XX/XXXX, when an earlier Bill Pay service of mine was inactivated, they sent a clearly titled " Activity Alert : Service Inactivation for Bill Pay '' - promptly, before any payment failed. In XX/XX/XXXX, when they reissued my debit card, they sent an " Activate Your New Card and Update Recurring Payments '' email - again, promptly, before anything broke. They have the capability, the template, and the established practice. They did not use any of it for the migration that damaged my credit. Whatever the reason, I was given no effective notice before the harm occurred. Bank of America has refused to correct the record I disputed both accounts directly with Bank of America. Their written responses : XX/XX/XXXX ( Case XXXX, Card XXXX ) : " We reported this account as delinquent for 30 days on XX/XX/XXXX. All of the account details we reported are accurate. We have completed our research and consider your dispute resolved. '' XX/XX/XXXX ( Case XXXX, Card XXXX ) : " We're reporting this account has never been delinquent. '' XX/XX/XXXX ( Case XXXX, Card XXXX ) : " Unfortunately, we're unable to change the information we reported to your credit file as you requested. We researched the delinquency and didn't find any errors. '' XX/XX/XXXX ( Case XXXX, Card XXXX ) : " The delinquency you inquired about either does not reflect on this account, or it was not 30 or more days past due. '' These responses answer a question I did not raise. I do not dispute that the payment was late- it was. I dispute that it is fair or accurate to report it as a derogatory mark when the lateness was caused entirely by Bank of America cancelling my six-and-a-half-year autopay without notice. Their investigation confirmed only that the payment was late and ignored the documented, bank-caused reason for it, along with the complete absence of any warning. Under FCRA 623, a furnisher 's investigation must be reasonable ; confirming the bare fact of lateness while disregarding the cause does not reasonably address the dispute I actually raised. There is a notable irony in those four letters : each one reached my address on file without difficulty. When Bank of America wished to deny my request, the mail arrived reliably. When they were obligated to warn me that my autopay had failed and my credit was at risk, that same address received nothing. I am separately filing disputes with XXXX XXXX, and XXXX under FCRA 611. I bring this complaint to the CFPB because Bank of America has already refused me in writing, and I anticipate the same automated re-verification through the bureau process unless the actual basis of my dispute is addressed. Current status Card XXXX still shows " 30-59 Days Past Due '' across all three bureaus over a {$10.00} balance - the mark Bank of America has refused to remove, and the focus of this complaint. Card XXXX shows no late payment ; Bank of America 's own letter confirms it " has never been delinquent. '' Both balances are now {$0.00}. Regulations that appear relevant Regulation E ( 12 CFR 1005.10 ) : A financial institution may not unilaterally terminate a preauthorized recurring payment without proper notice. A generic " your statement is available '' email that does not mention the cancellation does not satisfy this requirement. Regulation Z : Bank of America delivered periodic statements, but a statement is only meaningful notice if the consumer has reason to believe their payment method still functions. Sending routine statements while silently cancelling the autopay meant to satisfy them created a false impression of normal operation. E-SIGN Act : Electronic disclosures must be delivered through channels the consumer can reasonably access. Bank of America used my working email for everything else ; app push alerts presume an app I never installed ; mail, per my provider, never came. FCRA 615 ( a ) : Consumers must be notified before negative information is furnished to the bureaus. I was not. A competitor notified me - a day after the reporting had already occurred. FCRA 623 : Bank of America 's investigation of my direct disputes did not reasonably address the substance of what I disputed. UDAAP ( Dodd-Frank 1031 ) : Cancelling a 6.5-year autopay arrangement without effective notice, then reporting a {$10.00} late payment on a 13-year spotless account, is an unfair and abusive practice that caused substantial, unavoidable harm. A broader concern I do not believe my experience is isolated. The class action XXXX v. Bank of America Corporation ( Case No. XXXX, XXXX. XXXX. ) concerns the same practice of autopay cancellation without notice, and numerous consumer reports describe the identical pattern following this migration. I respectfully ask the CFPB to consider whether Bank of America 's migration notifications were adequate, how many customers were affected, what the bank is doing to proactively correct the credit reports it damaged, and why frontline staff repeatedly characterized a bank-caused system failure as the customer 's responsibility. Customers with fewer resources to fight this - those without the time to make repeated calls, record them, and assemble their own records- are being marked down for something Bank of America did to them. Requested resolution 1. Full deletion - complete removal, not a " disputed '' notation - of the 30-day late payment on Card XXXX from XXXX XXXX and XXXX. 2. Confirmation that Card XXXX is fully clear of any dispute notation, given that Bank of America has confirmed in writing it was never delinquent. 3. A written acknowledgment from Bank of America that the late payment was caused by their XX/XX/XXXX payment system migration, suitable for sharing with business partners or employers during the recovery period. 4. Reversal of any fees or interest arising from this incident. 5. A goodwill credit in recognition of the time required - multiple customer service calls and a written dispute process to resolve a bank-side error- and the ongoing impact to my credit standing. 6. Written confirmation when each correction is processed. 7. Investigation and proactive remediation for other customers affected by the migration in the same way. I have preserved all supporting evidence : Bank of America 's complete email history ( over 1,000 messages dating to XXXX ), recordings and transcripts of the XX/XX/XXXX and XX/XX/XXXX calls, the XX/XX/XXXX XXXX XXXX XXXX alert, all four of Bank of America 's written dispute responses, my credit reports from all three bureaus, and six and a half years of autopay confirmations. I am ready to provide any of it. I spent thirteen years building my credit record and never missed a payment. The single late mark on it exists only because Bank of America cancelled my autopay without notice - not because of anything I did. I am asking that it be removed.

Consumer complaint narrative: I am reporting misconduct by Chase, the national bank and credit card issuer that is part of JPMorgan Chase. Several months ago, I was perusing merchant offers available for my Chase credit card. I saw there were two offers available that applied to the same merchant. One offered {$10.00} cash back for spending {$50.00} or more at XXXX, and the other offered {$5.00} cash back for doing the same. Because I had not seen Chase simultaneously provide multiple offers for the same merchant before, I did the responsible thing and carefully read the terms and conditions to determine if combining offers was disallowed. The fine print said nothing about that, so I saved both offers and proceeded with a XXXX order that met the criteria. But I received only the {$10.00} credit. The {$5.00} credit remained missing. I contacted Chase customer service about this error, and what followed has been a months-long stream of lies and nonsensical claims with some hostility sprinkled in -- and the stunning willingness to burn decades of customer goodwill -- all over {$5.00} when Chase is XXXX in the wrong. The crux of their argument is that an excerpt from the merchant-offer terms and conditions that states " Offer valid XXXX time only '' means multiple offers can not be combined. That is an obvious lie, as no reasonable person would read it that way. " Offer valid XXXX time only '' is standard merchant-offer language that means an offer can't be used repeatedly on multiple purchases. It means nothing about multiple offers applying to a single purchase. I have explained this to customer service many times now. Further, Chase has repeatedly stated that they can not issue me the missing {$5.00} credit, even as a " goodwill gesture, '' because they have to treat all customers equitably. I have replied that I am not asking for special treatment, because any cardholder who had both offers saved should have received both credits. I have repeatedly explained the simple remedy : revise future merchant-offer language to explicitly state that offers can not be combined. I will honor and respect what is clearly written in the terms and conditions. But because that language was not included in these offers at the time I used them, Chase owes me the missing {$5.00} credit. But as I said at the beginning, this isn't about {$5.00} ; it's about accountability, transparency, and decency. This is about a bank claiming their terms and conditions state something they clearly don't, and when that lie is called out, repeatedly doubling down on it rather than admitting the obvious truth, making amends, and revising future offer language to reflect their intent. Worse, one of my early attempts to resolve this was via a phone conversation with an agent on the Chase " escalation team '' who literally hung up on me mid-sentence while I calmly pushed back on his attempts to gaslight me with the claim that " Offer valid one time only '' means " Offers can not be combined. '' I know it was not a dropped call because I heard him talking over me and saying he was going to hang up. That's shockingly unacceptable unprofessional behavior from any organization towards a customer who is firmly but calmly making their case and refusing to accept a lie. I have mentioned this incident multiple times in my subsequent messages to Chase customer service, and it has not even been clearly acknowledged, let alone apologized for. That alone is incredible. If all of this reflects how Chase does business and trains their customer-facing employees, it reflects a systemic problem at the XXXX of the company. The fact that they are willing to exhibit such ugly behavior over a mere {$5.00} only highlights the sheer absurdity. I certainly wouldn't trust them to handle anything of greater value.

Consumer complaint narrative: On XX/XX/year>, I was charged {$260.00} by XXXX XXXX on my Capital One XXXX credit card for a prepaid excess baggage service on an XXXX XXXX XXXX XXXX ). Upon arrival at the final destination ( XXXX ) on XX/XX/year>, my checked baggage was found to be irreparably damaged. I filed a damage report with the receiving carrier 's baggage partner ( XXXX XXXX ) on XX/XX/year>, the day of arrival, which is the standard procedure for XXXX XXXX where baggage is checked through to the final destination. I disputed the {$260.00} charge with Capital One. Capital One initially ruled in my favor and issued a credit. On XX/XX/year>, Capital One reversed this decision and rebilled the {$260.00}, citing XXXX XXXX 's chargeback rebuttal. XXXX XXXX 's rebuttal stated only that the baggage service was " fully utilized '' and that no damage report was filed with them directly. Neither point holds up. On the first point : " fully utilized '' means the bag was physically transported, but that does not mean the service was completed as contracted. A prepaid baggage service carries an implied obligation to deliver the bag in a reasonably intact condition at the final destination. My bag arrived with a broken hard-shell and a destroyed wheel, classified as irreparable by a repair expert appointed by the airline itself. A service that destroys the item it is contracted to transport has not been fully delivered. By XXXX XXXX 's logic, an airline could transport a bag in pieces and still claim the service was rendered. On the second point : this was an XXXX XXXX with baggage checked through to the final destination ( XXXX ). Under the XXXX XXXX, XXXX have the right to file damage claims against the final carrier upon delivery of baggage. I exercised this right exactly as intended, filing a damage report with the final carrier 's baggage partner on the day of arrival. XXXX XXXX 's assertion that no report was filed with them specifically does not negate a properly filed claim against the receiving carrier. Expecting a passenger to simultaneously file with every carrier on a multi-leg XXXX XXXX is neither standard practice nor reasonable. XXXX XXXX 's claim that no report was filed with them is therefore irrelevant, not exculpatory. I want to specifically highlight Capital One 's handling of this dispute as a failure of their chargeback process. I provided documented evidence of damage, a timestamped damage report filed the day of arrival, and third-party written confirmation of irreparable damage from the carrier 's own baggage partner. Capital One reversed their initial decision, which was correct, based solely on a merchant rebuttal that does not address the actual claim. XXXX XXXX cited a cancellation policy in response to a damage dispute. These are not the same thing, and a basic review of the documentation would have made that clear. This is not an isolated incident. This is the second time this year that Capital One has reversed an initial ruling in favor of a merchant after I submitted supporting documentation. In both cases, the merchant 's rebuttal was non-responsive to the actual basis of the dispute. Capital One appears to be rubber-stamping merchant rebuttals without conducting a meaningful review of the cardholder 's evidence. This raises serious questions about whether Capital One is fulfilling its obligations under the Fair Credit Billing Act to conduct a reasonable investigation before siding with a merchant. I am a cardholder in good standing who followed every required step. I disputed promptly, provided documentation, and responded within deadlines. Capital One 's process has failed me twice. I am filing this complaint because cardholders should not have to escalate to a federal regulator to receive the basic protections their credit card is supposed to provide.

Consumer complaint narrative: I am filing this complaint against Discover Card, issued by Discover, a division of XXXX XXXX XXXX, because Discover is treating an old identity-theft claim like a brand-new matter and is shifting the burden back onto me even though a sworn FTC Identity Theft Report already identified the Discover account as fraudulent. Discover then tells me to complete and return another Affidavit of Identity Theft with supporting documents within 10 days of receipt to continue the investigation. This is not a new identity-theft claim. My FTC Identity Theft Report number XXXX, signed under penalty of perjury on XX/XX/XXXX, already identified a fraudulent Discover account under account number XXXX. That FTC report states that I did not recognize the account, that it was the result of identity theft and fraud, and that the fraudulent items should be removed and collection activity should cease. Discover was on notice or should have been on notice long before XX/XX/XXXX. My CFPB complaint XXXX, filed XX/XX/XXXX, specifically named a Discover account opened on XX/XX/XXXX under account number XXXX as identity-theft information and attached the FTC identity-theft affidavit package XXXX XXXX response in that complaint says it contacted the data furnishers for the disputed items and asked them to verify the information. That means Discover or XXXX XXXX should not now act like this is the first time the Discover identity-theft claim was raised. Before Discover relies on the same excuses again, I want to address them directly. Discover should not claim that it needs a brand-new affidavit before it can take my identity-theft claim seriously. I already have a sworn FTC Identity Theft Report identifying the Discover account as fraudulent. Asking me to complete another company-specific affidavit a year later appears duplicative, delay-based, and designed to shift the burden back onto me instead of resolving the identity-theft claim. Discover should not claim that the account is valid merely because it has my name, address, Social Security number, date of birth, phone number, or other identifying information. Identity theft often involves real consumer information. Identity matching is not proof that I opened, authorized, used, benefited from, ratified, or accepted liability for the account. Discover should not claim that its transaction list proves liability. The XX/XX/XXXX affidavit packet includes a list of transactions and payments, including XXXX, Dollar General, Caseys, XXXX, XXXX, XXXX, XXXX payments, and payment representments. A transaction list is not proof that I opened the account, received the card, activated the card, authorized the charges, benefited from the charges, or knowingly accepted liability. Discover should not treat payments or payment representments as automatic ratification. Payment activity does not prove that I knowingly opened, authorized, used, benefited from, ratified, or accepted liability for the account. Identity theft can involve compromised payment sources, stored credentials, automated payments, or account access by someone other than the consumer. Discover must prove authorization, not merely point to payment activity. Discover should not use local merchant names as proof of liability. Transactions appearing near where I live do not prove that I personally made them. Discover must provide actual evidence, such as application records, identity-verification records, device records, IP address records, card-delivery records, card-activation records, merchant-level evidence, signatures, camera evidence if available, and payment-source verification. Discover should not claim that no current Discover credit-report entry means there is no harm. My Experian report dated XX/XX/XXXX showed no Discover charge-off, no Discover collection, no closed accounts, no collections, no inquiries, and XXXX accounts ever late. My later credit reports also do not show a Discover negative account, yet Discover is still sending identity-theft paperwork in XXXX for an account it says it is investigating. That is confusing, unresolved, and concerning because it suggests Discover may still be maintaining, collecting, investigating, or preserving liability on an account previously identified as identity theft. Discover should not keep this account open, unresolved, collectible, transferable, or capable of future reporting while demanding more paperwork from me. Discover has had more than enough notice to investigate the identity-theft claim and either provide real proof of liability or close and block the account as fraud. This conduct appears unfair, deceptive, and potentially fraudulent by omission because Discover is implying that my investigation depends on submitting another affidavit, while omitting that a sworn FTC Identity Theft Report already identified the Discover account as fraudulent in XXXX and that the dispute was already raised through the CFPB/Experian process. I dispute the Discover account ending in XXXX, the related Discover account number XXXX, all alleged balances, all alleged transactions, all alleged payments, all payment representments, all fees, all interest, all collection activity, all furnishing, all account status information, and any claim that I opened, authorized, used, benefited from, ratified, or accepted liability for this account.

XX/XX/year> at XXXX XXXX : The company initiated a second call from XXXX. An agent identified herself as collecting on behalf of the bank. XX/XX/year> at XXXX XXXX : The company initiated another telephonic collection contact to my wireless line. They have failed to provide the legally demanded validation files, ignored explicit oral and written directives to cease collection activities, used deceptive local number spoofing tactics, transmitted unauthorized settlement text messages during an active dispute window, and engaged in telephonic harassment. I request that the CFPB compel this company to cease all collection and reporting activities immediately and administratively dismiss this facially corrupted account.

Summary of Misrepresentation : The merchants website advertises this " XXXX XXXX '' using images that depict a roll of flexible tape. Based on these professional images, a consumer reasonably expects a product with the properties of tapespecifically flexibility and adhesion. However, the product received is functionally useless : The product page for the " XXXX XXXX XXXX XXXX XXXX '' presents a fundamental conflict between its marketing title and technical specifications. While the title prominently uses the word " Metallic, '' which implies a high-sheen, reflective, and brilliant finish, the body text contradicts this by describing a " soft satin finish. '' In the context of professional cake decorating, these terms represent two entirely different aesthetic tiers. A bank claim can be supported by the argumen t of Material Misrepresentation, as the merchant used a high-value descriptive keyword to trigger a sale while delivering a product that lacks the primary light-reflective properties promised in the heading. Furthermore, there is a significant discrepancy regarding the product 's structural performance. The primary marketing photograph depicts the ribbon as a rigid or semi-rigid material capable of holding sharp, upright loops and architectural folds on a cake. Conversely, the description labels the material as " soft and flexible '' edible lace. Physics dictates that a soft, lace-like material can not maintain the structural integrity shown in the photo without internal support, which is not mentioned. This constitutes Deceptive Visual Advertising, as the consumer is induced to purchase based on a " structural '' use case that the actual physical material is incapable of performing. The listing further fails the consumer by utilizing subjective terminology in place of technical dimensions. By labeling the ribbon as " Wide '' without providing specific measurements in inches or millimeters, the merchant creates a " dimensional ambiguity '' that makes it impossible for a professional to determine if the item is fit for their specific project. In banking disputes, this is categorized as a Failure of Disclosure. Without exact specifications, the term " Wide '' is a subjective claim rather than a factual description, leading to a purchase of an item that may not meet the necessary physical requirements for the intended application. Transparency regarding safety is also a major fault, as the page lacks a visible ingredient list or allergy warning. For an edible product, particularly one using XXXX and metallic pigments, which often contain iron oxides or specific dyes ( like XXXX XXXX ), the omission of this data is a critical safety gap. The bank 's argument for Non-Disclosure of Essential Safety Information is highly effective here ; a consumer can not be expected to accept an " edible '' product if they can not verify its contents against dietary restrictions or legal food safety standards prior to the transaction. Finally, the merchant employs a restrictive " No Returns '' policy for food items, which conflicts with their categorization of the item as " Equipment and Supplies. '' This creates a " Liability Shield '' where the merchant avoids accountability for the products failure to perform, like the equipment shown in the photos. A bank claim can argue that this is an Unfair Trade Practice, as the merchant is using the " food '' classification to bypass consumer protection rights when the product fails to meet the " professional grade '' quality standards they advertised. By proving the product is materially different from its description, the merchants " No Return '' policy becomes legally unenforceable in a dispute. 1. Misleading " Metallic '' Representation The primary selling point is the " Metallic '' finish, but the merchant includes a contradictory fine-print disclaimer. The XXXX : The product name explicitly uses the word " Metallic, '' yet the description admits it is " not as metallic '' as their other products and compares it to a " soft satin ''. This is a bait-and-switch tactic where the title promises a high-shine finish that the merchant knows the product can not achieve. My argument : " The merchant 's own documentation admits the product does not meet the standard defined by its own title. This is deceptive advertising. '' 2. Unfair " No Returns '' Policy for Defective Goods XXXX XXXX XXXX typically refuses returns on edible items regardless of quality. If the ribbon looks like matte plastic or dark grey rather than " XXXX XXXX, '' I should claim Visual Misrepresentation. Property Theft : Credit card rewards points possess a defined, contractually backed monetary value. This was an outright theft of my earned property hosted on Chases digital platform.

Consumer complaint narrative: I am submitting this complaint because American Express has repeatedly failed to provide evidence supporting its refusal to award a promised welcome offer after I fully satisfied the spending requirements and paid the annual fee associated with the card. '' This statement is entirely conclusory and unsupported by evidence. In my responses to American Express, I specifically addressed each category referenced in its explanation and requested that the company provide the factual basis, records, documentation, account history, or other evidence supporting its determination. American Express either refused or was unable to provide any documentation demonstrating why I was deemed ineligible for the welcome offer. Importantly, during the application process, I did not receive any warning, notification, or pop-up message indicating that I was ineligible for the welcome offer. American Express utilizes an eligibility notification system that is designed to inform applicants before they complete an application if they are not eligible for a welcome offer. Had I received any such notice, I would have had the opportunity to decide whether to proceed with the application. No such warning was provided to me. As a result, I reasonably relied on the advertised offer when applying for the card, paying the approximately {$700.00} annual fee, and directing more than {$8000.00} in spending to the account in order to satisfy the stated requirements. It is fundamentally unfair for American Express to accept my application, collect the annual fee, benefit from my spending activity, and then retroactively deny the promised welcome offer based on undisclosed criteria that were never communicated to me before or during the application process. American Express has now been given multiple opportunities through two separate CFPB complaints to provide evidence supporting its determination and has failed to do so each time. Rather than supplying documentation, records, or specific facts supporting its position, it has repeatedly relied on the same generic and unsupported statement. American Express is effectively asking the CFPB and me to accept its conclusion without evidence while retaining the benefit of my business, the annual fee, and the spending activity required to earn the offer. I believe this conduct raises significant concerns regarding transparency, fairness, and potential unfair or deceptive practices. Consumers should not be induced to apply for a credit card through a specific promotional offer, satisfy all stated spending requirements, pay substantial annual fees, and then be denied the promised reward based on undisclosed criteria that can not be substantiated when challenged. I respectfully request that the CFPB require American Express to do one of the following : 1 ) Produce the specific records, documentation, account history, eligibility analysis, internal decision-making records, and other evidence that formed the basis for its determination that I was ineligible for the XXXX Membership Rewards point welcome offer ; or 2 ) Award the XXXX Membership Rewards points as originally promised after I satisfied the spending requirements associated with the offer ; or 3 ) Refund the approximately {$700.00} annual fee. If American Express can not produce evidence supporting its determination, I believe its refusal to honor the advertised offer constitutes an unfair and deceptive practice that falls squarely within the CFPB 's consumer protection mandate. The CFPB was established to protect consumers from unfair, deceptive, or abusive acts and practices and to promote transparency in consumer financial products. I am requesting the CFPB 's assistance in ensuring that American Express is held accountable for either substantiating its decision with evidence or honoring the promotional offer that induced me to obtain and use the card. I appreciate the CFPB 's assistance and request a substantive response supported by evidence rather than another generic statement that does not explain the basis for American Express 's actions.

Consumer complaint narrative: I am filing a formal complaint against SoFi for an unauthorized account debit resulting from a check encoding error, and for a subsequent refusal to honor federal and state banking regulations regarding properly payable items. On XX/XX/year>, a check I wrote to my landlord for rent cleared my SoFi checking account. The check was written and authorized for the exact amount of {$1600.00}. However, the payee 's depository bank mistakenly requested, and SoFi incorrectly disbursed, an altered/over-encoded amount of {$2600.00}. This resulted in an unauthorized over-debit of exactly {$1000.00} from my personal funds. When I identified the discrepancy and contacted SoFi customer support to dispute the unauthorized transaction, SoFi refused to credit my account or initiate a formal adjustment request through the clearinghouse network. Instead, SoFi representatives instructed me to contact the payee 's financial institution to recover my funds. Under Uniform Commercial Code ( UCC ) 4-401, a payor bank may only charge a customer 's account for items that are properly payable according to the original tenor of the drawer 's order. SoFi has a clear regulatory obligation to reimburse my account for the unauthorized {$1000.00} debit and utilize the interbank adjustment process to claim the overpayment from the presenting bank. SoFi can not legally delegate this institutional responsibility to the consumer. A digital image of the cleared check, clearly displaying the authorized legal amount of {$1600.00}, is attached to this complaint.

XXXX creditors including banks exercising right of set-off generally can not seize funds from a husband and wifes joint bank account ( tenancy by the entireties ) to pay a debt owed by only XXXX spouse. While [ TILA ] ( 15 U.S.C. 1601 ) regulates consumer credit disclosures and rescission rights, the shielding of joint assets from individual debts is a specific, robust feature of XXXX common law known as " tenancy by the entireties ''. Abusive practices in banking " set off '' ( using funds in XXXX account to cover debt in another ) occur when institutions leverage gaps in consumer understanding, unequal bargaining power, or consumer reliance to take unreasonable advantage. Consumer Financial Protection Bureau Complaint Company : Wells Fargo Bank Related Claim ID : XXXX Related Executive Escalation Reference : XXXX Related CFPB Complaint Reference : XXXX Complaint Category : Investigation Process / Complaint Handling / Inconsistent Findings Complaint Narrative : This complaint concerns Wells Fargo 's handling of the investigation process itself and the changing factual basis used to support denial of my fraud claim. My original complaint involved unauthorized debit-card transactions totaling approximately {$15000.00} including resulting fees. However, the focus of this complaint is not simply the denial of reimbursement. Rather, it concerns the consistency, accuracy, and reliability of the investigative process utilized to reach that determination. Throughout the handling of the matter, Wells Fargo systems and representatives reflected materially different transaction counts and records. During the course of the investigation, I was presented with approximately 27 transactions, 30 transactions, 35 transactions, and ultimately 39 disputed transactions identified through reconciliation efforts. Because the underlying disputed transaction records changed depending on the representative, department, or system being reviewed, I became concerned regarding the reliability of the data used to support the investigative conclusions. Additionally, Wells Fargo 's written denial specifically stated : " The shipping address provided to the merchant for the disputed transaction ( s ) matches your address on file. '' When I challenged that statement, I explained that the address maintained on file with Wells Fargo was my mother 's residence and that I do not routinely receive packages or merchandise shipments at that address and have not done so for years. Following that challenge, the explanation provided by Wells Fargo changed from shipping address matching to billing address matching. These are materially different facts. A shipping address concerns where merchandise is delivered. A billing address concerns payment verification. As a result, I am unable to determine which factual basis was actually relied upon during the investigation. I also received an executive-level review following my original CFPB complaint. During those discussions, I was advised that the claim had been denied. However, after being informed of the denial, I was then asked multiple additional investigative questions regarding possession of the card, possession of the PIN, access to the account, and related issues. This created additional confusion because it is unclear why substantive investigative questions were still being asked if the determination had already been finalized. Conversely, if the investigation remained ongoing, it is unclear how the matter could already be considered closed. Another concern involves the investigative factors relied upon to support denial. Wells Fargo repeatedly referenced factors including : Continued possession of the physical card ; Continued possession of the PIN ; Geographic similarity ; Merchant similarity ; Digital-card activity ; and Android-device activity. However, the matter also involved a documented impersonation event in which an individual posing as a Wells Fargo representative possessed substantial account-specific information, including personal identifying information and card-related information. During that impersonation event, I was advised that an alleged unauthorized user had been added to the account and was associated with a telephone number utilizing the same XXXX area code as my own number. This raises concerns regarding the degree of weight placed upon geographic-pattern analysis and other account-association indicators when evaluating sophisticated account-compromise scenarios. Additionally, Wells Fargo has repeatedly referenced digital-card and Android-device activity as a basis supporting denial. However, I have not been provided documentation explaining how Wells Fargo determined that the device involved belonged to me rather than an unauthorized actor possessing compromised account information. My concern is that several factors cited in support of denial appear to demonstrate association with an account rather than authorization by the account holder. I am requesting review of Wells Fargo 's investigative and complaint-handling process, including : inconsistent transaction records; changing factual explanations ; conflicting shipping-address and billing-address rationales ; post-denial investigative activity ; the factual basis supporting device attribution conclusions ; and whether the investigative methodology utilized was sufficiently reliable and internally consistent under the circumstances presented. Requested Resolution : I request an independent review of Wells Fargo 's investigative process, the factual basis relied upon in support of denial, and the consistency of the records and explanations provided throughout the handling of this matter. I also request that Wells Fargo be required to clearly identify the specific evidence relied upon to support its conclusions and address the inconsistencies outlined above.

Consumer complaint narrative: I am filing this complaint regarding Capital Ones handling of my dispute involving a {$55000.00} charge to XXXX XXXX on XX/XX/year>. I hired XXXX XXXX for a commercial tenant improvement project for XXXX XXXX XXXX. The contractor received three payments totaling {$68000.00}. I am not disputing all of those payments. I specifically excluded the {$4100.00} payment because I acknowledge that some limited preliminary work was completed. My dispute relates only to the XX/XX/year> payments totaling {$64000.00}, including the {$55000.00} charge processed through Capital One. Before I signed the contract, XXXX represented that the project would be completed around XXXX XXXX. I relied on that representation when authorizing payment and moving forward with the project. By XXXX XXXX, the project was nowhere near completion. The work remained limited to early-stage demolition and partial framing while substantial portions of the contracted scope remained unfinished. Major contract items including plumbing rough-in, electrical rough-in, concrete and footings, drywall, doors, trim, paint, and completed usable suites were not delivered as represented. Throughout the project, I repeatedly requested updates, accounting of funds paid, project status information, and an orderly transition when it became clear the project would not be completed as promised. I requested itemized accounting so that payments could be reconciled against completed work. The requested accounting was never provided. I remained willing to resolve the matter professionally and communicated that position in writing. Instead of providing the requested accounting and continuing toward resolution, the contractor stopped work and treated my request as a breach. I was ultimately forced to retain a replacement contractor and incur additional costs to complete substantial unfinished portions of the project. I submitted extensive documentation to Capital One, including payment records, project communications, permit records, photographs, requests for accounting, proof of my efforts to resolve the dispute directly with the contractor, and multiple supplemental dispute letters. I also submitted additional information after Capital Ones initial denial. When I contacted Capital One for clarification, I received differing explanations regarding the denial. I was advised that additional information was needed and that proof of a refund or confirmation from the merchant was required. I could not provide such proof because the merchant disputed my position, never agreed to issue a refund, never issued a refund confirmation, and never provided the requested accounting. Requiring documentation from the merchant who was the subject of the dispute effectively made it impossible to satisfy Capital Ones request. Capital One ultimately denied the dispute and stated only that the information provided was insufficient to validate my claim. The denial letter did not clearly identify what information was missing, did not explain why the extensive documentation submitted was inadequate, and did not explain how Capital One evaluated the evidence demonstrating substantial non-performance of the contracted services. My dispute was never based on a claim that no work occurred. In fact, I specifically acknowledged that some work was performed and intentionally excluded one payment from the dispute. My dispute was based on the contractors failure to complete the contracted services as represented and failure to deliver the scope of work for which payment was made. I am also concerned that the explanation provided by Capital One representatives appears inconsistent with Capital Ones published dispute guidance. Capital Ones public dispute information states that disputes may be filed when a customer paid for a service and did not receive it, only received part of it, or when the service was not delivered as described. My dispute falls squarely within those categories. I never claimed that no work occurred. Rather, I claimed that I only received a limited portion of the contracted services and that the services delivered were not completed as represented. Additionally, Capital Ones published guidance identifies contracts, invoices, photographs, and communications with the merchant as relevant supporting documentation for dispute investigations. I submitted those categories of evidence. Despite doing so, Capital One did not explain why the evidence was insufficient, what additional information was required, or how its denial was consistent with its own published dispute standards. Based on the facts above, I believe Capital One failed to conduct a reasonable investigation, failed to provide a meaningful explanation for its denial, and failed to fairly evaluate the evidence demonstrating substantial non-performance of contracted services. I am requesting that Capital One conduct a full and independent review of the dispute, explain the specific basis for its denial, review all documentation previously submitted, explain how its decision is consistent with its published dispute guidance, and reconsider the dispute based on the evidence demonstrating that the contracted services were not completed as represented.

Consumer complaint narrative: I am filing this formal complaint against Bank of America for failing to properly investigate billing disputes, violating consumer protection rights, shifting investigative burdens to the consumer, and wrongfully refusing to close my account.1. Improper Investigation & Shifting Excuses on Hotel DisputeBank of America denied a dispute for a {$72.00} hotel charge for " services not rendered. '' Their handling of this dispute has been deceptive and contradictory. First Dispute : Bank of America claimed the charge was " valid, '' despite already having the exact dates of the alleged stay and being told I never used the room. Second Dispute : The bank reversed its excuse and denied the claim by falsely stating I " did not provide information. " This is completely untrue. I explicitly provided Bank of America with the hotel 's direct contact information. Under federal consumer protection laws, it is the bank 's legal obligation to conduct a reasonable investigation, which includes contacting the merchant when provided with their details. The hotel 's records clearly show I never checked into the property. Furthermore, I possess timestamped video evidence proving I slept inside my rental vehicle that night. Bank of America simply refused to do its job, ignored the evidence, and used lazy shifting excuses. 2. Gross Negligence in Investigating Obvious Double ChargesIn a separate instance, I experienced an explicit double charge and disputed both transactions because it was unclear which one was the error. Bank of America denied my dispute. Upon reviewing the case, I discovered that the merchant had sent Bank of America the exact same receipt for both charges, featuring identical transaction ID numbers and identical timestamps. Bank of America 's dispute department rubber-stamped the denial without even looking at the merchant 's paperwork. I had to catch this blatant error myself because the bank failed to review the very evidence sitting in their own file. 3. Violation of Regulation DD ( Truth in Savings Act ) & Official Account Disclosures Bank of America has been continuously assessing unauthorized monthly maintenance fees on my account. My original account terms explicitly stated that the monthly fee would be waived with a recurring monthly deposit of at least {$500.00}, a condition I consistently met. Bank of Americas official Deposit Agreement states that they will inform customers of modifications to fees and terms prior to the effective date. Furthermore, under Federal Regulation DD ( Truth in Savings Act ), the bank is legally required to provide at least 30 days ' advance written notice before changing terms that increase a consumer 's fee liability. Bank of America completely failed to provide any such notice via paper, email, or digital statement disclosure, resulting in unlawful and predatory fee deductions. 4. Refusal to Close the AccountBecause of this continuous poor service and lack of security, I moved all of my funds out of the bank. I have requested that my account be permanently closed. Bank of America is refusing to allow me to close the account, keeping it open solely to accumulate further fees and force me to pay back disputed funds that I do not owe.

At no point did she offer to inspect the installation, repair the work, or discuss a remedy. I attempted in good faith to resolve the issue directly with the merchant before filing a dispute. Consumer complaint narrative: I am submitting a new complaint regarding the banks handling of my unauthorized transaction claim because the banks prior response did not comply with RegulationE. This is not a duplicate complaint. This complaint concerns the banks procedural noncompliance, unsupported factual assertions, and failure to provide the documentation required under XXXX XXXX XXXX. In its denial letter, the bank stated that I confirmed the transactions via XXXX on XX/XX/XXXX and confirmed again by phone on XX/XX/XXXX, and that the transactions were authorized based on transaction and account history, location, and pattern of use. Without access to the actual evidence, I can not meaningfully understand, evaluate, or appeal the banks determination. This is similar to being asked to respond to a decision in a legal proceeding without being given the evidence used to reach that decision. RegulationE requires the bank to provide copies of the documents it relied upon, and I am simply requesting the information necessary to review and respond to their findings. The only other documentation the bank provided was : ( 1 ) a list of transactions, which is not evidence of authorization, and ( 2 ) an outsourced Visa investigation packet for a single {$330.00} transaction. I am including this detail so the CFPB is aware that I attempted to provide every form of documentation reasonably available to me. In addition, I made a goodfaith effort to stabilize the account by moving my savings to cover approximately half of the overdraft created by the unauthorized transactions. I did this to prevent further fees and demonstrate that I was not attempting to avoid responsibility for the account while the dispute was pending. This situation has caused significant and ongoing stress, largely because I have been unable to obtain the evidence necessary to understand or respond to the banks determination. I have made every goodfaith effort to resolve the matter, but the lack of transparency has made it difficult to move forward. Finally, I am concerned that the bank issued provisional credit before completing its investigation. The sequence of events raises questions about whether the investigation was completed in a reasonable and compliant manner.

Goldman Sachs Bank USA 's response to that complaint requested closure on the grounds that their investigation found no bank error and that I failed to provide sufficient evidence of return. This dispute concerns a transaction with merchant XXXX ( XXXX, XXXX, XXXX, XXXX ) on my Apple Card, Dispute Case No. XXXX, transaction date XX/XX/XXXX, in the amount of {$360.00}. I disputed this charge on XX/XX/XXXX, XX/XX/XXXX, XX/XX/XXXX, and XX/XX/XXXX. Goldman Sachs ruled in favor of the merchant each time. The facts are as follows : On XX/XX/XXXX, I contacted the merchant at XXXX to initiate a return of Order # XXXX. The item received was defective upon arrival, with a broken belt piece included in the shipment. On XX/XX/XXXX, the merchant responded with return instructions. Within that single email, the merchant twice instructed me to commit customs fraud by declaring the package value at under {$20.00}, despite the actual purchase price being {$360.00}. The instruction appeared first mid-paragraph : " please declare the package value under {$20.00}, which will be helpful to expedite the clearance '' and was then repeated as a standalone notice : " Important : Please declare the package value under {$20.00}, which will be helpful to expedite the clearance. '' This is customs fraud under 18 U.S.C. 542, a federal crime. Deliberately undervaluing a {$360.00} shipment as {$20.00} on a customs declaration is not a technicality or a cultural misunderstanding. It is a deliberate instruction to falsify a federal document. I refused to comply. Additionally, the merchant 's return shipping cost was nearly equivalent to the original purchase price, making the return economically impossible even setting aside the illegal customs requirement. Under the Fair Credit Billing Act, I am only required to make a good faith effort to return defective merchandise. I made that effort on XX/XX/XXXX and XX/XX/XXXX, in documented written communications. The merchant 's only return pathway required me to break federal law. No merchant terms and conditions supersede federal statute. This documented evidence, including the merchant 's XX/XX/XXXX email with the customs fraud instruction appearing twice, was submitted to Goldman Sachs during the dispute process and was also attached to CFPB Complaint No. XXXX. Goldman Sachs ' response to that complaint does not reference, acknowledge, or address this evidence in any way. A financial institution that receives documented proof of a merchant instructing a consumer to commit federal customs fraud and proceeds to rule in that merchant 's favor four consecutive times has conducted a materially incomplete investigation and has failed its obligations under the FCBA. I am also requesting that the CFPB examine whether Goldman Sachs has a broader pattern of failing to properly review consumer-submitted evidence in transaction disputes of this nature. If their investigation process allowed customs fraud documentation to be submitted, reviewed, and dismissed four consecutive times in a single case, it is reasonable to conclude that other consumers may have experienced the same outcome. A systemic failure to engage with evidence of illegal merchant conduct would represent a serious institutional compliance issue that warrants regulatory scrutiny beyond my individual dispute. I am requesting the following : 1. That the CFPB escalate this matte r and not accept Goldman Sachs ' prior closure as resolution. 2. That Goldman Sachs be directed to conduct a new investigation that specifically addresses the customs fraud instruction documented in the merchant 's XX/XX/XXXX email. 3. That the {$360.00} charge be permanently credited to my account. 4. That the CFPB consider whether Goldman Sachs ' dispute review process warrants a broader examination for similar consumer complaints. I was on XXXX XXXX military service during a significant portion of this dispute period and pursued this matter diligently despite those obligations. I have now been fighting this for over seven months across four dispute rounds and one prior CFPB complaint. The evidence is documented, specific, and unambiguous. I am asking the CFPB to hold Goldman Sachs accountable for ignoring clear proof of illegal merchant conduct.

Consumer complaint narrative: This complaint concerns three consecutive billing disputes on my OnePay XXXX XXXX issued by Synchrony Bank. Federal law gives consumers the right to a reasonable investigation of a disputed charge and a clear written resolution stating what was decided and what it means for their account. Across three consecutive disputes I have received neither a completed investigation nor a clear final answer. What I have received are letters that describe an ongoing process, a portal that contradicts the letters, and in one case a letter that calls itself a resolution while pointing to a temporary credit as its only evidence without ever stating what was decided or what happens to my money. A resolution requires a closed file a statement of what was investigated, what was found, and what it means for the account with no conditions attached. What Synchrony has provided instead are letters that describe a process still in motion, using conditional language that preserves their ability to reverse the credit at any time. DISPUTE 1 {$110.00} ( XX/XX/XXXX ) : I filed a dispute on XX/XX/XXXX. On XX/XX/XXXX, the institution issued a temporary credit letter characterizing the adjustment as subject to reversal pending further review. No final determination followed. I made repeated contacts, including a chat on XX/XX/XXXX ( Ref # XXXX ) and a call with a supervisor on XX/XX/XXXX, neither of which produced a resolution. On XX/XX/XXXX, I filed a CFPB complaint ( Case XXXX ). Only after that federal complaint was filed did the institution issue a letter dated XX/XX/XXXX stating we have completed our review. That letter does not state what the investigation concluded or what the decision means for the credit on my account. It points to the temporary credit applied on XX/XX/XXXX as if that act constitutes a resolution but that same credit had been characterized as subject to reversal since the day it was issued. The letter also cites the CFPB filing date as the sole inquiry date while omitting documented contacts on XX/XX/XXXX and XX/XX/XXXX that preceded it. The account portal shows two entries for this dispute one marked Dispute Completed and one marked Under Review. A consumer looking at their own account can not determine from that whether the dispute is closed or still open. There is no written correspondence that resolves that contradiction. DISPUTE 2 {$130.00} ( XX/XX/XXXX ) : I filed a dispute on XX/XX/XXXX. On XX/XX/XXXX, the institution issued a temporary credit letter using identical language to the {$110.00} dispute characterizing the credit as subject to reversal pending further review. No final determination was ever issued. The written record stops at the temporary credit letter. As of XX/XX/XXXX, this dispute has been open for 91 days, exceeding the maximum investigation period permitted under federal law, and no final determination has been issued. The account portal shows two entries for this dispute for the same date and amount one marked Dispute Completed and one marked Under Review. A consumer looking at their own account can not determine from that whether the dispute is closed or still open. There is no written correspondence that resolves that contradiction. DISPUTE 3 {$70.00} ( XX/XX/XXXX ) : I filed a dispute on XX/XX/XXXX. The institution acknowledged the dispute on XX/XX/XXXX and committed in writing to provide the outcome within 60 days. As of XX/XX/XXXX, that deadline has elapsed. The only written correspondence I have received is a letter dated XX/XX/XXXX characterizing the adjustment as a temporary credit subject to reversal. The institution has not provided the outcome it committed to provide. The account portal shows this dispute as Under Review. This institution has demonstrated across three consecutive disputes that a final written determination only materializes under pressure, arrives with facts selectively presented, or never arrives at all. Dispute 1 required a federal complaint to produce any final letter, and that letter distorted the timeline by omitting documented prior contacts and pointed to a temporary credit as a resolution without stating what was actually decided. Dispute 2 has no final letter the written record stops at the temporary credit. Dispute 3 blew past the institutions own committed deadline with nothing but a temporary credit letter that still leaves the door open to reversal. Synchrony has demonstrated a consistent pattern of avoiding clear, timely, final written determinations and when one is finally forced, presenting a selective account of the facts rather than a straight answer about what was decided and what it means for the consumers account.

What is it?

How it happens
Phishing (pronounced "fishing") or Smishing
This is when fraudsters send reputable-looking emails or text messages trying to trick you into providing
personal information or infecting your device with malware.
Hacking
This is when a thief gains access to your personal information by using technology to break into your
computer, devices or network.
Spoofing
These are bogus websites or phone numbers that look legitimate and ask you to provide personal
information.
Stealing
A thief takes your mail, personal documents, financial statements, laptop, smartphone or other device.
How to help minimize the risk
 Be vigilant with your documents, devices and property.
 Never provide your personal information to someone who calls, texts or emails you.
 At minimum, have unique passwords for your financial accounts and don't use them across multiple
sites.
 Regularly check your credit report to monitor for changes you didn't anticipate.
 Sign up for free credit score and identity monitoring with Chase Credit Journey and get alerts for

bureaus to investigate and resolve the activity. Consider adding a freeze or fraud alert. A fraud alert will notify
others that you might be a victim of fraud, while a freeze prevents the use of your credit without your
approval.XXXX XXXX XXXX XXXX XXXX XXXX XXXX XXXXReach out to local law enforcement
 Supply all the information you can, including exact dates, times and account numbers.
 File a police report if advised.
 Save a copy of the police report because some businesses or financial institutions may require it to
remove any fraudulent charges.
Report your identity theft to the Federal Trade Commission
 The FTC is dedicated to protecting U.S. consumers.
 Go to their website, identitytheft.gov, to file a report and get a recovery plan.
 When you file a report, the FTC and other agencies use your information to build cases against
scammers.
Tighten up your security
 Change the user names and passwords on all of your active accounts. Have unique passwords for
your financial accounts, and don't use them across multiple sites. Consider using a password
manager to create and store strong passwords.
 Keep your phone, computer and web browsers current, as there are often security patches included
with system updates.

Consumer complaint narrative: I am submitting this complaint regarding Capital One 's repeated practice of immediately removing newly deposited funds intended for essential household expenses and doing so during non-business hours when consumers have no meaningful opportunity to contact the bank before the funds are taken. I have been a Capital One customer since approximately XXXX and have maintained my relationship with the bank for over a decade. The events giving rise to this complaint occurred on the evening of XX/XX/XXXX. My mother sent me money through XXXX specifically to pay her portion of our XXXX home internet bill. This was not employment income or discretionary spending money. It was money designated for an essential household utility payment that was due by XXXX p.m. that night. After receiving the money, I transferred it into my Capital One savings account and immediately logged into XXXX to make the payment. Before I could complete the payment, Capital One removed the funds from my savings account almost immediately after they were deposited. The timing of this transaction is one of the primary reasons for my complaint. The funds were removed at approximately XXXX p.m., outside of normal business hours, leaving me with no meaningful opportunity to speak with a representative, explain that the money was intended for an essential utility payment, or request assistance before it was taken. I was actively on XXXXXXXX XXXX website attempting to pay my bill when I discovered that the money my mother had just sent had already been removed from my account. The pattern of Capital One 's actions is what concerns me. For weeks, both my checking account and my savings account remained with only nominal balances. Those balances remained untouched during that entire period. More recently, I moved those small balances, leaving approximately {$2.00} in my checking account. Those funds remained in my checking account without being removed. However, the moment my mother sent approximately {$40.00} through XXXX for an essential household utility bill and I transferred those funds into my savings account, Capital One immediately removed the newly deposited money. The small balance that had existed for weeks remained untouched while the newly received family assistance intended for an essential utility payment was removed almost immediately. This is not the first time this has happened. In XXXX, Capital One immediately removed money that my mother had sent to my checking account. I filed a complaint with the Consumer Financial Protection Bureau regarding that incident. That complaint resulted in Capital One returning my funds, and the matter was closed after the company responded. During my recent telephone conversation with Capital One, I directed the representative to review the notes from the prior complaint. While reviewing the account history, the representative read aloud that the previous reversal occurred because " the customer requested to do so. '' This demonstrates that Capital One previously exercised discretion to restore the funds after my request. I also explained during that call that I am currently experiencing severe financial hardship, am pursuing an XXXX matter, recently qualified for XXXX XXXX receive XXXX benefits, and rely on my mother 's assistance to help maintain essential household expenses. My XXXX internet connection is one of my primary means of communicating with my attorneys and managing ongoing legal matters. I respectfully request that the Consumer Financial Protection Bureau investigate this repeated pattern and require Capital One to explain why nominal balances remained untouched for weeks while newly deposited family assistance intended for an essential household utility was immediately removed. I also request that Capital One restore the funds and review its practices regarding immediate after-hours removal of newly deposited money so that consumers are provided meaningful notice or an opportunity to communicate before essential household funds are taken. The attachments submitted with this complaint include documentation of my XXXX XXXX XXXX account balance and service status, current Capital One account activity, prior Capital One account activity showing the previous reversal, and the prior CFPB complaint information demonstrating the repeated nature of this issue.

Retaliatory Account Restriction ( UDAAP ) : The deliberate removal of my historical billing statements ( XXXX and XXXX ) and transaction history from my online portal immediately following my initiation of XXXX XXXX. Credit Reporting Violations ( FCRA 1681s-2 ( b ) ) : The furnishing of a mathematically impossible balance, a fabricated account closure status, and a false " High Credit '' limit. Importantly, my case establishes the exact procedural posture required for a private right of action under 15 U.S.C. 1681s-2 ( b ). District courts clearly articulate three elements for this claim, all of which are met here : ( 1 ) The consumer sent notice of disputed information to a consumer reporting agency : I submitted XXXX separate disputes through XXXX ( not just directly to Wells Fargo ). ( 2 ) The consumer reporting agency then notified the defendant furnisher of the dispute : XXXX transmitted Automated Consumer Dispute Verifications ( ACDVs ) to Wells Fargo, successfully acting as the filtering mechanism and indirect-dispute trigger that activates 1681s-2 ( b ) duties. ( 3 ) The furnisher failed to investigate reasonably : Across all XXXX ACDVs, Wells Fargo blindly verified the inaccurate data and refused to correct the errors. Explicit Statement Regarding Prior Investigations : I explicitly state that Wells Fargos prior investigations and responses are entirely unsatisfactory, in bad faith, and legally deficient. The Wells Fargo Enterprise Complaints Management Office ( ECMO ) and Stakeholder, Agency, Government & Executive Office ( SAGE ) have completely failed to conduct the reasonable, substantive, human investigations required by federal law. Instead of addressing incontrovertible mathematical proofs or reviewing external XXXX XXXX XXXXXXXX ACH logs, Wells Fargo has systematically abused the regulatory complaint portal by mass-closing inquiries with irrelevant, boilerplate templates ( including bizarre references to " auto loans '' and " paper envelopes '' in credit card disputes ). They are actively using the existence of an arbitration claim as an improper shield to avoid conducting standard ledger audits and to avoid fulfilling their duties as a data furnisher under 15 U.S.C. 1681s-2 ( b ). Arbitration Deflection and Non-Waivable FCBA Duties : In their recent resolution letters, Wells Fargo 's SAGE office explicitly refused to respond to these issues, claiming that the matters will be addressed through arbitration and that they " will not respond to the issues outside of that process. '' This arbitration deflection is legally invalid. The FCBA imposes independent, non-waivable statutory obligations under 15 U.S.C. 16661666j. Wells Fargo 's unilateral statement that it will not respond to issues outside of arbitration does not extinguish its pre-existing duty to investigate a properly lodged billing error dispute. Under 15 U.S.C. 1666, Wells Fargo is legally required to conduct an actual investigation and either correct the error or provide a written explanation detailing the reasons they believe the account was correctly shown. Wells Fargo has completely failed to meet this statutory investigation requirement. Non-Discretionary FCBA Timing and Resolution Pathways : Furthermore, the FCBA imposes specific, non-discretionary duties on a creditor upon receipt of a proper billing error notice. I triggered these duties by providing timely written notice detailing my name, account number, the exact date, type, and amount of the missing {$6000.00} payment, along with the reasons for my belief that an error occurred. The office manager personally assisted with the credit application and set up the automatic payments. We were assured that the payments would be split evenly and structured so the promotional balance would be paid in full before the promotional period ended.
