Consumer complaint narrative: On XX/XX/XXXX, I became aware that something unusual was happening with my bank account. While I was at work, I began receiving text messages and phone notifications containing security codes and authentication requests that I had not initiated. At the time, I was not attempting to log into my online banking account, make any transfers, change any account settings, or conduct any banking activity. Because I was occupied with work responsibilities, I was unable to immediately investigate the issue in detail. However, I recognized that receiving security codes without requesting them could indicate that someone was attempting to access my account. As the day continued, I became increasingly concerned when I noticed activity involving my account that I did not recognize. Once I returned home from work, I immediately contacted PNC Bank to report what I believed was fraudulent activity. During my conversation with the bank, I learned that unauthorized changes had been made to my account information. Specifically, the phone number associated with my account had been changed without my knowledge or authorization. This discovery confirmed my suspicion that an unauthorized individual had gained access to my account. The fact that my phone number had been altered is particularly important because it appears that the individual who gained access to my account used this change to bypass security measures and gain control over account communications. By changing the phone number, the individual prevented me from receiving important security notifications and may have enabled themselves to receive authentication codes intended to protect my account. During my call with PNC Bank on XX/XX/XXXX, I informed the representative that I had not authorized any of the transactions in question and that I believed my account had been compromised. The bank initiated a fraud claim and dispute regarding the unauthorized transactions. I acted immediately upon discovering the issue and did everything within my power to notify the bank and protect my account. In addition to contacting the bank, I also contacted local law enforcement on the same day. A police report was taken documenting the incident. My goal was to ensure that the matter was formally investigated and that there would be an official record showing that I reported the fraud immediately upon discovering it. I understood the seriousness of the situation and wanted to cooperate fully with both the bank and law enforcement authorities. After the initial report, I waited for the banks investigation to be completed. Several weeks later, I contacted PNC Bank to obtain an update regarding the status of my claim. At that time, I was informed that the claim had been denied. According to the explanation provided to me, the bank concluded that the transactions were not eligible for reimbursement because they involved XXXX transfers and because the transactions were allegedly authorized. I strongly disagree with that conclusion. I did not authorize these transactions. I did not initiate the transfers. I did not approve any changes to my account information. Most importantly, I reported the incident immediately after discovering it. The fact that a third-party payment platform such as XXXX was used does not change the fact that the underlying account access was unauthorized. After receiving notice of the denial, I contacted law enforcement again to follow up on the status of the investigation. During that conversation, I learned that a new detective had been assigned to the case. The detective informed me that little or no meaningful investigation had been conducted previously and that additional investigative steps would now be necessary. As a result, I was advised that the investigation would continue and that further time would be required before any conclusions could be reached. More recently, I received a letter from PNC Bank explaining the basis for the denial of my claim. The letter indicated that the bank relied on what it described as a historical pattern of use in determining that the transactions were authorized. I was extremely concerned and frustrated by this explanation because it does not address the key facts surrounding the account takeover. The critical issue is not whether I have used my account or XXXX in the past. The critical issue is that unauthorized access occurred, my phone number was changed without my permission, authentication codes were generated that I did not request, and fraudulent transactions were conducted while I was actively attempting to stop the unauthorized activity. These facts strongly suggest that my account security was compromised by someone other than myself. I subsequently contacted both PNC Bank and XXXX seeking additional information and assistance. Unfortunately, each organization directed me back to the other. XXXX advised that PNC Bank possesses the investigative information and account records. PNC Bank, meanwhile, emphasized that XXXX is a third-party service. As a result, I have been left without meaningful answers regarding who accessed my account, how the unauthorized changes occurred, where the funds were sent, and why my claim was denied despite the evidence that an account takeover occurred. I respectfully request a complete review of this matter. Specifically, I request that all records related to the investigation be reexamined, including account access logs, IP addresses, device information, phone number change records, authentication records, transaction details, and any evidence relied upon to conclude that the transactions were authorized. I also request that the bank consider the fact that I reported the fraud immediately, filed a police report, cooperated fully with all requests, and consistently maintained that I did not authorize these transactions. My objective is simple : to determine where my money went, identify the individual responsible for accessing my account, and recover the funds that were taken without my authorization. I believe the facts support my position that this was an unauthorized account takeover and not a transaction that I knowingly or willingly approved.

I am submitting this complaint regarding a pending account closure scheduled by WesBanco. The institution has communicated that my business banking relationship will be closed within approximately 30 days. This closure decision was represented as being based entirely on a specific internal allegation regarding conduct attributed to me. I dispute the accuracy of this allegation and do not accept it as fact. To my knowledge, the allegation is not supported by objective account activity, transactional records, or independently verifiable documentation. During the relevant period, I maintain residences in multiple locations and was residing abroad for an extended period consistent with that arrangement. I returned to Maryland on XX/XX/XXXX. During this period, I was not in a position to directly manage or immediately respond to banking communications or operational issues in real time. This is part of an established multi-residence living arrangement that necessarily limits immediate responsiveness to banking inquiries and does not reflect disengagement from the account relationship. Separately, during this same period, I experienced significant and unresolved issues with account access and transaction processing. These issues materially disrupted normal business banking operations, including my ability to reliably monitor, access, and manage funds and transactions in support of ongoing business obligations. This occured between approximately XX/XX/XXXX until XX/XX/XXXX, when I returned. I was out of the country before the service interruption. The alleged statement forming the basis of the closure is disputed in its entirety. The communication in question occurred with my spouse present in the vehicle, and the call was conducted on speaker for its duration. I do not believe the allegation reflects an accurate or reliable characterization of what occurred, and I am not aware of any objective documentation supporting the interpretation that has been attributed to me. Based on the information available to me, I understand the institutions decision to initiate closure to be based solely on this disputed allegation rather than on documented account behavior, transactional history, or objective financial risk indicators. There has been no clear presentation of account-based evidence demonstrating that normal banking activity or risk-based criteria support this adverse action. This pending closure and the underlying circumstances are causing and will continue to cause significant and potentially irreparable harm to my business operations, financial continuity, and professional reputation, given the reliance of ongoing business activities on uninterrupted access to banking services and the downstream impact of adverse banking determinations on third-party relationships. This complaint requests supervisory review limited to whether the pending closure is supported by verified and documented account activity, whether appropriate evidentiary standards were applied prior to initiating closure of an active business account, whether account access and transaction handling during the relevant period were properly managed and documented, and whether any internal determinations relied upon are substantiated by objective facts tied to account behavior rather than unverified assertions. Additionally, review is requested to determine whether the adverse action process reflects fair, consistent, and properly documented banking practices consistent with applicable regulatory expectations for business account relationships. The requested outcome is a written explanation of the factual and documented basis for the closure decision, identification of the specific account activity relied upon for the adverse action, a full review of account access and transaction handling during the relevant period, correction of any unsupported internal determinations if identified, and confirmation that any closure action is grounded in verified facts and consistent with fair banking standards.

Consumer complaint narrative: On XXXX XXXX XXXX, my XXXX debit card was used to pay a {$170.00} charge at XXXX XXXX XXXX XXXX in XXXX, Tennessee. The hotel processed a refund of {$170.00} back to the same card on XX/XX/XXXX, at XXXX XXXX confirmed by the hotel 's folio and by the XXXX merchant transaction record ( both already provided to the bank ). The refund never appeared in my account. On or about XX/XX/XXXX, I called the bank by phone to notify it of this disputed transaction. My authorized representative also called the bank the same day, separately, on my behalf. The representatives on both calls handled by two different bank reps on the same day advised us NOT to file a formal dispute, stating that doing so would " make it take longer '' or " elongate the refund. '' This consistent advice, delivered to two separate callers by two different representatives on the same day, steered me away from formally invoking my Regulation E rights at the moment notice was actually given. The fact that the same advice was given by separate representatives on the same day suggests this was not an isolated rep error but a practice or scripted response. Under 12 C.F.R. 1005.11 ( b ) ( 1 ), oral notice of a Reg E error triggers the bank 's investigation obligation. The bank may require written follow-up only if it informs the consumer of that requirement at the time of the oral notice which is the opposite of what the bank 's representatives did on XX/XX/XXXX. The 10-business-day window from the XX/XX/XXXX oral notice has now elapsed, and the bank has issued no provisional credit. The bank has subsequently stated, in email correspondence, that the dispute could take " 60120 days '' because the bank was " waiting on the merchant to respond. '' This response conflates two separate processes : the XXXX chargeback / back-end merchant settlement process ( which can run 60120 days ) and the consumer 's rights under Regulation E ( which require the bank to either complete its investigation within 10 business days or provisionally credit the disputed amount under 12 C.F.R. 1005.11 ). The 60120 day chargeback timeline is not a permissible basis to withhold provisional credit on the front end. The documentation already provided to the bank shows that the merchant issued the refund on XX/XX/XXXX, with an authorization number, token, and invoice number. The dispute is not about whether the merchant will refund the merchant has refunded. The question is where that refund went between the merchant 's processor and my account, which is precisely the type of error Regulation E provisional credit is designed to address during investigation. I am filing this complaint regarding three concerns : 1. The bank 's discouragement of a formal dispute filing on XX/XX/XXXX advice given consistently to two separate callers on the same day by different representatives. This pattern steered me away from exercising my Regulation E rights and may constitute a deceptive practice under UDAAP. I am specifically requesting that the Bureau ask the bank whether the " don't file/ it will take longer '' advice was a scripted, trained, or otherwise institutional response, as the consistency of the advice across two different reps on the same day suggests it was not an individual error. 2. The bank 's conflation of merchant chargeback timelines with Regulation E provisional credit obligations, which is being used as a stated reason to withhold provisional credit my account is entitled to under 12 C.F.R. 1005.11 ( c ). 3. The bank 's failure to follow Regulation E error-resolution procedures, including the failure to disclose my right to a formal dispute at the time of the XX/XX/XXXX oral notice. Relief requested : ( a ) immediate provisional credit of {$170.00} to my account pending completion of the investigation, as required by 12 C.F.R. 1005.11 ( c ) ; ( b ) a written explanation of the bank 's Regulation E procedures and whether the XX/XX/XXXX " don't file '' advice reflects scripted or trained representative responses ; and ( c ) any further corrective action the Bureau deems appropriate. Documents available and previously provided to the bank : the hotel folio dated XX/XX/XXXX ; the XXXX XXXX Transaction Manager record confirming the XX/XX/XXXX refund authorization ; email correspondence with the bank 's representative.

I believe American Express failed to provide accurate information regarding its own policies and failed to properly address my repeated requests for supervisory review. I am requesting that American Express review the handling of my account, review the customer service interactions and chat transcripts, explain why I was repeatedly provided inaccurate information regarding reinstatement, explain why my requests for managerial escalation were not honored, and provide a clear and accurate explanation of the companys position regarding account reinstatement and the impact, if any, of the pending financial review on that determination.

Consumer complaint narrative: I am filing this complaint regarding two unauthorized or unexplained security incidents on my American Express account, and Amex 's failure to communicate any findings or resolution after 20 days, in apparent violation of their investigative obligations under Regulation E ( Electronic Fund Transfer Act ). Incident 1 : Unauthorized Voice Payment, XX/XX/year> On XX/XX/year>, an unauthorized voice payment was made on my American Express account via Amex 's automated pay-by-phone system. The payment was for the minimum balance due. My account is set up for automatic full statement balance payment via ACH from my linked checking account, which processes automatically a few days after the statement date. I have not made a phone payment on any credit card in more than a decade and did not initiate this payment. I reported this unauthorized electronic fund transfer to American Express on XX/XX/year>. As of XX/XX/year>, 20 days later, I have received no findings, no explanation, and no communication regarding the outcome of that report. Incident XXXX : Unsolicited SMS Payment Link, XX/XX/year> at XXXX I received an SMS message from American Express 's verified number at XXXX on Saturday XX/XX/year> stating " Amex : Here is the link you requested to make a payment. '' I did not request any payment link. When I contacted Amex about this message, they confirmed they have no record of a payment link being generated or sent for any of my cards. The origin of this SMS remains unexplained. Following this call, Amex closed and reissued my card. I have received communication confirming the new card is being sent, but still no findings or update on the XX/XX/XXXX unauthorized voice payment. Security Vulnerability I Am Reporting I personally tested Amex 's pay-by-phone system after these incidents and documented the following authentication chain when calling from a phone number associated with the account : the system asks for the last 4 digits of the Social Security Number, then the last 5 digits of the Amex card number, then offers to process a payment using the linked checking account on file, including stating the bank name and last 4 digits of the checking account. This authentication chain is exploitable through the following means, all of which are readily accessible to bad actors : First, phone number spoofing technology is widely available and free, allowing anyone to spoof a call from a victim 's associated phone number, which grants access to the easier authentication path. Second, the last 4 digits of Social Security Numbers are widely available through numerous large-scale data breaches affecting data brokers, government agencies, and financial institutions, including breaches that affected individuals who never directly interacted with the breached entity. Third, American Express card numbers follow a known, structured format. The last XXXX digits of a card number are not random and can be derived or bypassed via automated brute-forcing or scripted enumeration against the IVR phone system. My affected card was newly issued in XX/XX/year>, making it highly unlikely to have appeared in a legacy data breach, which further supports the conclusion that the card number was obtained through automated brute-forcing or scripted enumeration rather than a breach. The result is that a bad actor with spoofing capability and access to commonly breached personal data can authenticate into Amex 's pay-by-phone system and initiate ACH payments from a victim 's linked checking account without the account holder 's knowledge or consent, and without triggering any out-of-band verification such as a one-time passcode or push notification. What I Am Requesting I am requesting that the CFPB compel American Express to provide the following : XXXX. A full explanation of how the XX/XX/year> voice payment was authenticated, including what verification the caller passed and whether phone number spoofing was considered as the entry point. XXXX. A formal response to the XX/XX/year> SMS payment link that Amex 's own representatives can not account for. XXXX. An explanation of what steps Amex is taking or will take to address the structural authentication vulnerability in their pay-by-phone system described above, given that knowledge-based verification relying on SSN digits and predictable card number formats is no longer a meaningful security barrier in the current data breach environment. 4. A statement confirming whether Amex 's automated pay-by-phone system utilizes telecom attestation data to verify the legitimacy of the incoming Caller ID before granting access to the reduced verification path. I have made multiple good faith attempts to resolve this directly with American Express and have received no substantive response after 20 days.

In XX/XX/XXXX, I purchased a mattress for approximately {$2500.00} and enrolled in a 24-month deferred interest promotional financing plan. At the time of purchase, I understood this promotion to mean that if any balance remained at the end of the promotional period, interest would begin accruing on the remaining balance going forward. I was not aware that interest was accruing retroactively during the promotional period and would be applied in full if the balance was not paid off completely within 24 months. I set up autopay and consistently made all required minimum monthly payments. However, the minimum payment amounts were variable and decreased significantly over timefrom approximately {$97.00} per month down to as low as {$41.00}. When the promotion expired, Synchrony Bank applied approximately two years of backdated interest at an APR of 29.99 % in a single billing cycle. As a result, my account balance increased dramatically from {$1100.00} to {$2600.00} in one month. This increase was entirely due to retroactive interest charges that I did not reasonably expect based on my understanding of the promotion. The use of the term deferred interest is misleading, as it suggests that interest is postponed rather than accruing in the background and applied retroactively as a lump sum. Had I clearly understood that failing to pay off the balance in full would result in the application of all accrued interest, I would have paid the remaining balance before the promotional period ended. Additionally, the structure of declining minimum payments appears to contribute to this issue by allowing balances to remain higher for longer periods, increasing the likelihood that consumers will not pay off the balance in time and will incur retroactive interest charges. Consumer complaint narrative: Subject : Request for Regulatory Investigation into Cash App 's Consumer Protection Practices To Whom It May Concern : I am requesting a formal review and investigation into Cash App 's handling of accidental transfers and its apparent lack of meaningful consumer protections for users who suffer financial losses due to honest mistakes. My husband, XXXX XXXX XXXX, mistakenly sent {$500.00} to the wrong Cash App user. Upon realizing the error, we immediately submitted a refund request through the Cash App platform. The recipient declined the request and retained the funds despite knowing they were not the intended recipient. What is most troubling is not merely the recipient 's refusal to return money that does not belong to them, but Cash App 's complete unwillingness to assist in resolving the matter. When we contacted customer service, we were effectively told that nothing could be done and that our only option was to pursue Small Claims Court. This response shifts the entire burden onto the victim while allowing both the platform and the recipient to avoid accountability. As consumers, we are encouraged to trust digital payment platforms with our hard-earned money. Yet Cash App appears to provide no meaningful safeguards when an obvious mistake occurs. A transaction involving hundreds of dollars can be completed in minutes, leaving little opportunity for a sender to correct an error. Once the recipient refuses a refund request, the sender is left with no practical remedy. This raises several serious concerns : Why does Cash App not have a mandatory review or recovery process for disputed accidental transfers? Why are recipients permitted to knowingly retain funds sent in error without any investigation by the platform? What monitoring exists to identify users who repeatedly receive and refuse to return mistaken payments? Why is there no meaningful escalation process for consumers who suffer financial losses due to accidental transfers? How does Cash App define its responsibility to protect customers who use its platform in good faith? Cash App possesses transaction records, account information, device information, and user identification data. Yet the company appears unwilling to use these resources to facilitate resolution when consumers report mistaken payments. Instead, consumers are directed to courts, creating a costly and burdensome process that many individuals can not reasonably pursue. My concern extends beyond my family 's loss of {$500.00}. I am concerned for every consumer who may find themselves in the same position. A financial platform should not be designed in a way that allows a person to knowingly keep money that was sent in error while the rightful owner is left without assistance. I respectfully request that regulators examine whether Cash App 's policies adequately protect consumers and whether additional safeguards should be required, including : Enhanced recipient verification before transfers are finalized. Longer cancellation or reversal periods for large-dollar transactions. A formal dispute resolution process for accidental payments. Investigation of recipients who knowingly retain funds sent in error. Stronger consumer protections for digital payment platforms operating in the United States. Consumers deserve more than a message stating, " There is nothing we can do. '' We deserve a payment platform that values fairness, accountability, and the protection of honest customers. Thank you for your attention to this matter and for your commitment to protecting consumers. Respectfully, XXXX XXXX On behalf of XXXX XXXX XXXX

Consumer complaint narrative: I am filing this formal complaint against American Express for failing to conduct a reasonable, good faith investigation into a billing error, which violates my consumer rights under the Fair Credit Billing Act ( FCBA ), 15 U.S.C. Section 1666. 1. Nature of the Billing Error : The transaction involves a bait-and-switch scheme by the merchant, XXXX XXXX XXXX XXXX and XXXX XXXX The hotel front desk explicitly marketed and sold a " Tacos and Margaritas Night '' experience, promising unlimited tacos and margaritas for a fixed price of {$50.00} per person. Relying entirely on this verbal agreement, I made a reservation. Upon arrival at the restaurant on XX/XX/year>, we were seated and served appetizers before being handed a physical menu. This menu revealed the actual price was {$55.00} per person and explicitly stated that margaritas were excluded and sold separately. When we attempted to leave due to this clear misrepresentation, hotel staff informed us we would be charged a mandatory no-show fee. Because the property is in an isolated location and it was late, we were held to the reservation under financial duress. The goods delivered were not as described ; the food quality was entirely substandard, and the pricing structure completely contradicted the agreement made at the time of the transaction. The following morning, I made a good faith attempt to resolve the issue with local management, who refused to assist. 2. Failure of American Express to Investigate Under the FCBA : Under 15 U.S.C. Section 1666 ( b ) ( 3 ), a billing error includes any reflection on a statement of goods or services not delivered in accordance with the agreement made at the time of the transaction. I timely disputed the {$140.00} charge with American Express under the " goods or services not as described '' category. American Express closed its investigation and rebilled my account on XX/XX/year>, based solely on the merchant 's submission of a copy of the physical menu and a signed payment voucher. American Express concluded that my signature on the voucher constitutes voluntary acceptance of the charge. By relying exclusively on the merchant 's paper trail, American Express completely failed to investigate the core of my dispute : Failure to evaluate duress : American Express ignored evidence that the signature on the voucher was obtained under financial duress via the threat of a predatory hotel no-show fee. Failure to evaluate the timing of the contract : The binding agreement was formed at the front desk when the reservation was sold, not when the merchant modified the terms after seating us. Violation of 15 U.S.C. Section 1666 ( a ) ( B ) ( ii ) : The FCBA requires a creditor to conduct a meaningful investigation before determining a charge is correct. Rubber stamping a merchant 's standard paperwork while actively ignoring a consumer 's documentation of deceptive trade practices and forced compliance does not constitute a lawful, thorough investigation. 3. Remedy Requested : I request that the CFPB compel American Express to properly fulfill its regulatory obligations under the Fair Credit Billing Act. The documentation provided by the merchant merely confirms that a transaction occurred, which I have never denied. It does not validate the deceptive trade practices used to capture the transaction. I request a full reversal of the rebilled {$140.00} charge.

Consumer complaint narrative: On XX/XX/XXXX, I incurred a medical charge of {$2800.00} through CareCredit after seeking treatment at XXXX XXXX in XXXX XXXX, Tennessee. My monthly automatic payment was approximately {$45.00} and was successfully withdrawn each month. The promotional period expired on XX/XX/XXXX. At the time of expiration, my promotional balance was approximately {$1300.00}. The XX/XX/XXXX statement showed a deferred interest amount of {$1700.00} associated with the promotional purchase. The following statement reflected a sudden interest charge of {$1800.00}, causing my balance to increase from {$1300.00} to {$3100.00} despite no new purchases being made. My automatic payment also increased from approximately {$45.00} to {$110.00}, which was withdrawn on XX/XX/XXXX and caused an overdraft in my bank account. This was the event that alerted me to the existence of the retroactive deferred interest and the dramatic increase in my balance. After discovering the retroactive interest charges, I contacted Synchrony Bank and requested assistance. During that conversation, I was informed that Synchrony could only provide a courtesy extension until XX/XX/XXXX because, according to the representative, company policy and applicable credit-reporting requirements limited extensions to within approximately 30 days of the promotional expiration date. I found this response particularly troubling because I was not meaningfully alerted to the issue until after my automatic payment was withdrawn on XX/XX/XXXX. My monthly automatic payment had historically been approximately {$45.00}, but the XX/XX/XXXX withdrawal increased to {$110.00} and caused an overdraft in my bank account. Only after that withdrawal did I become aware of the retroactive interest charges, the expired promotional period, and the dramatically increased account balance. Synchrony then effectively informed me that I had only until XX/XX/XXXX, less than XXXX week later, to come up with approximately {$1300.00} to pay off the remaining promotional balance and avoid the retroactive interest. Following Wells Fargo 's investigation, I was informed that Wells Fargo had determined that no wrongdoing had occurred and declined to reimburse the fees, other than a single {$15.00} refund. I disagreed with this conclusion and requested escalation because the investigation appeared to focus solely on whether the fees were technically authorized under account terms rather than whether Wells Fargo representatives had provided inaccurate or incomplete information that caused the fees to occur. The representative placed me on hold to double check, returned to the call, and informed me clearly that if my account received at least {$500.00} in qualifying electronic deposits during the month of XXXX, a monthly service fee would not be charged. My concern is that Wells Fargo 's investigation failed to meaningfully address the central issue : whether Wells Fargo representatives provided inaccurate or misleading information that caused me to incur fees that I otherwise would have avoided.

As a consumer, I reasonably believed that promotions displayed to me within my authenticated American Express account were applicable to my account. I had no reason to believe otherwise. In fact, the purpose of logging into a customer account is to receive information and offers that are relevant to that specific customer relationship. My complaint is not based on a disagreement with the existence of terms and conditions. Rather, it is based on the fact that American Express presented these promotional benefits to a logged-in customer whose card type was already known to the company. A reasonable consumer should not be expected to assume that prominently displayed promotional benefits shown within a personalized booking experience do not apply to them. Nor should consumers be expected to search through extensive terms and conditions to determine whether American Express is displaying benefits for which they are ineligible despite knowing the card product associated with the account. The advertised benefits were material to my purchasing decision. Had I known that I would not receive the advertised {$600.00} statement credit, the anticipated XXXX rewards earnings, and the {$250.00} hotel property credit, I would have reevaluated my options and may have booked directly with the hotel or through another provider. These benefits represented a significant portion of the overall value proposition that influenced my decision to proceed with a prepaid reservation exceeding {$5700.00}. After discovering that I would not receive the advertised benefits, I made multiple good-faith attempts to resolve the issue directly with American Express XXXX On XX/XX/year>, I initiated an online chat with American Express. During that conversation, the representative informed me that the benefit was associated with what they described as " the XXXX XXXX '' and indicated that my XXXX XXXX XXXX XXXX was not eligible. Before any meaningful discussion or resolution could occur, the chat session was disconnected. I then called American Express customer service seeking clarification and assistance. The representative I spoke with was unable to assist and advised that I would need to speak with American Express XXXX. When I requested escalation to a manager, the call was disconnected. I called a third time and ultimately spoke with a supervisor named XXXX. During that conversation, XXXX acknowledged that he understood how a reasonable consumer could be confused by the manner in which the promotion was presented. He recognized that the advertising and booking experience could lead a cardmember to believe they were eligible for the advertised benefits. However, despite acknowledging the confusion, XXXX advised that the only resolution he could offer was cancellation of the reservation. He stated that he was unable to provide any goodwill accommodation, statement credit, points adjustment, travel credit, or any other remedy. I do not believe cancellation alone is an adequate solution. I relied upon the advertised benefits when making my booking decision. American Express had the ability to identify my card type before displaying the promotion and before accepting my prepaid reservation. The burden should not be placed on consumers to discover exclusions hidden within terms and conditions when American Express already possesses the information necessary to determine eligibility and tailor promotional displays accordingly. I respectfully request that American Express review this matter and provide an appropriate resolution. At a minimum, I request consideration of a goodwill accommodation reasonably equivalent to the value of the benefits that were advertised and relied upon during the booking process. I further request that American Express review its marketing and booking practices to ensure that promotional offers are not displayed to logged-in cardmembers who are known to be ineligible for those benefits. Consumers should be able to rely on promotions displayed within their authenticated account experience without having to independently determine whether American Express is presenting benefits that do not apply to the account they are actively using. Thank you for your time and consideration.

I am not seeking to avoid my legitimate financial obligation I am seeking relief from a charge that I believe was inadequately disclosed and that Synchrony 's customer service refused to address in good faith.
